About: Wu Experiment — parity violation in ⁶⁰Co β decay

Concept
At very low temperature, the nuclear spins in a ⁶⁰Co source tend to point along a magnetic field. A beta detector above the source records one warming run with the field pointing up and another with it pointing down. Parity conservation means that an experiment and its mirror image must give the same result. The two runs test that statement.
Serves
Introductory modern physics units on beta decay, nuclear spin, and parity.
Inquiry
Record the beta rate while the cold source warms. Reverse the magnetic field, cool the source again, and repeat with the same detector. Compare the two curves and then compare the apparatus with its mirror image.
Model
The historical experiment included calibration and control measurements that are not modeled here.
PrincipleWhere it appears
Observe, then interpretEach question is answered from a completed run or from the mirror comparison.
TemperatureCooling increases the degree of spin alignment. Warming makes the spin directions random again.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Cool the source

⁶⁰Co → ⁶⁰Ni* + e⁻ + νe

At very low temperature, the ⁶⁰Co nuclear spins tend to point along the magnetic field. The beta detector is above the source. Record the first run as the source warms.

After the run: when the spins initially point toward the detector, how does the count rate compare with the warm rate?

2 · Reverse the magnetic field

Reverse the magnetic field and cool the source again. The nuclear spins now point away from the detector. The detector itself does not move.

After the run: what happens to the initial count rate when the field is reversed?

3 · Compare with a mirror

Parity conservation means that an experiment and its mirror image must give the same result. In a mirror, the electron direction reverses relative to the nuclear spin.

The two field directions produce different initial count rates. What does this show?

The Physics

Parity violation · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

In 1957 Chien-Shiung Wu and her colleagues tested whether nature treats a process and its mirror image alike, using the beta decay of cobalt-60 nuclei lined up by a magnetic field. This sim lets you repeat it: cool a crystal, count electrons in one detector, reverse the field, and compare.

What you'll learn

  • How the temperature of the crystal sets how well the nuclear spins line up.
  • How an electron's direction relates to the spin it came from, and what one fixed counter sees of it.
  • How two runs with opposite fields give one number, 𝒜, and how many counts it takes to trust it.
  • Why a mirror image of the experiment turns this into a test of parity.
One crystal, one counter, one field direction at a time.

What's on screen

  • Nuclear spins (purple arrows) and the net spin ⟨J⟩ arrow on the left, whose length is P. A ring means disordered.
  • Field B (teal arrow) from the solenoid rings.
  • β electrons (red dots with tails) and the grey counter above the crystal, with its running count.
  • Counting-rate plot (below the stage): rate ÷ warm rate, one point per historical minute; B ↑ blue, B ↓ orange. The dashed line at 1 is a warm source.
  • Detector counts panel: the first-minute rates, 𝒜, and its expected value.
See itRecord one run with the field up. Watch for: a blue trace building across the counting-rate plot, one point per historical minute.

Fixed in the sim: the decay (⁶⁰Co → ⁶⁰Ni* + e⁻ + ν̄e, with decay asymmetry A = −1), the counter (radius 0.95 cm, 2.0 cm above the source), and the temperature scale (P = 0.60 at 3 mK).

03

Why the crystal has to be cold

Nuclear spins start out pointing every which way. A magnetic field pulls them into line, thermal jiggling pushes them back out, and the alignment depends on the balance. The sim measures it by P, the average spin component along B divided by the full spin: P = 0 is random, P = 1 is perfectly aligned. For ⁶⁰Co, which has spin 5:

P = B5(C/T)
B5 is the Brillouin function for spin 5. The sim sets C = 5.7 mK so that P = 0.60 at its coldest setting, 3 mK.
Alignment against temperature, on the slider's own log scale.
  • At 1 K, the opening value, P = 0.002. The sim draws the net spin as a ring above about 110 mK, where P falls below 0.02.
  • For P well below 1, P ≈ 0.4·C/T: halving T doubles P. At 10 mK, P = 0.22.
See itCool the crystal from where it is now down to 3 mK. Watch for: the net spin ring growing into an arrow along B as P rises.
04

Electrons favour the side opposite the spin

For an aligned ⁶⁰Co nucleus, the relative probability that the electron leaves at angle θ from the spin direction is

W(θ) = 1 + A · P · β · cos θ, A = −1, β = v/c
W = 1 means no preference. The sim uses A = −1 for this decay.
W at P = 0.60 and the average β = 0.49. A dashed circle (W = 1) is an unpolarized source.
  • With A = −1, electrons are less likely along the spin (θ = 0°) and more likely against it (θ = 180°).
  • The factor β means fast electrons are steered more strongly than slow ones. Averaged over the beta spectrum, β̄ = 0.49.
  • At P = 0.60, 43% of electrons leave into the hemisphere toward the spin and 57% into the opposite one.
Key idea. The preference is a property of each decay. What a real counter can see of it is the next section.
See itRecord a run with B ↑, so the spins point up at the counter. Watch for: the first blue points falling below the dashed warm-rate line.
05

From emission to count rate

The counter is a disc of radius 0.95 cm, 2.0 cm above the source, so it sees a narrow cone about the vertical (half-angle 25°). Compared with the same counter and an unpolarized (warm) source, its rate is

R = 1 + s · A · P · β̄ · Q
s = +1 for B ↑ and −1 for B ↓. Q = 0.95 is the average of cos θ over the counter's cone; a pinpoint counter on the axis would have Q = 1.

With A = −1 and β̄ · Q = 0.466, that is R↑ = 1 − 0.466 P and R↓ = 1 + 0.466 P. A warm source gives about 170 counts per recorded minute, the reference the sim divides by.

A run stands for 18 minutes of the real experiment, played in 26 s with one point per minute. The crystal starts at 3 mK, warms to 1 K by minute 6, and stays there while B stays fixed, so P falls and both rates drift toward 1:

minuteTPR↑R↓

2–310 mK0.220.901.10

See itRecord a B ↑ run, then a B ↓ run, at 4× speed. Watch for: blue points starting below the dashed line, orange points starting above it, and both settling onto it by about minute 6.
06

Two runs give one number, 𝒜

The sim compares the first minute of each run, when P is highest:

𝒜 = (R↓ − R↑) / (R↓ + R↑) = P · β̄ · Q ≈ 0.47 P
At P = 0.60, 𝒜 = 0.28. Even P = 1 gives only 0.47, because the electrons are not all fast and the counter is not a point.

Counts fluctuate by √N, so 𝒜 carries an error of about σ ≈ 1/√N. The two first minutes hold N ≈ 330 counts, so σ ≈ 0.05. A typical pair gives 𝒜 near the expected 0.27, within about 0.1 of it, and about 5σ from zero. Halving P halves 𝒜, so the same confidence takes four times the counts.

T

This is the sim's crystal-temperature slider; move it here and the apparatus follows. A real run warms during its first minute, so its expected 𝒜 is a little below the value at 3 mK.

See itRecord a B ↑ and a B ↓ run at 4× speed and let the sim compare them. Watch for: the measured 𝒜 within about two error bars of the expected value, usually several σ from zero.
07

The mirror argument

Reflect the experiment in a mirror (the sim's mirror turns x into −x). Momentum is a polar vector; spin and B are axial, so a reflection treats them differently: the electron's vertical momentum pz is unchanged, but Jz and Bz both reverse.

Polar and axial vectors under the sim's mirror. The product ⟨J⟩·p changes sign.
  • In the mirror image the counter is still on top, and the field and spin point the other way. It is a B ↓ apparatus drawn next to a B ↑ one.
  • If the decay law were the same in a mirror world, both would count the same. ⟨J⟩·p is a pseudoscalar: a term proportional to it, like A·P·β·cos θ, can exist only if parity is violated.
The real apparatus and its reflection. In the reflection the electrons would come out along the spin.

The sim's Mirror image switch draws this reflection to the right. Once both runs are recorded, a line at the bottom of the canvas reports whether the two rates differ by more than 2σ.

See itTurn on the mirror image at 3 mK with B ↑. Watch for: in the dashed right-hand panel, the B arrow and the net spin arrow point down while the counter stays on top.
08

Where it matters

  • Wu's experiment, 1957. At the National Bureau of Standards in Washington, Wu, Ambler, Hayward, Hoppes and Hudson aligned ⁶⁰Co nuclei at about 0.01 K and counted electrons while reversing the field (Phys. Rev. 105, 1413). The rate depended on the field direction. Lee and Yang, who proposed the test, won the 1957 Nobel Prize in Physics.
  • A left-handed weak force. The result led to the V−A theory, in which the weak interaction acts only on left-handed particles. In 1958 Goldhaber, Grodzins and Sunyar found the neutrino left-handed.
  • Today. Experiments measure the neutron's beta asymmetry (A ≈ −0.12, the same sign as in the sim) to find the axial coupling relative to the vector one.
Go deeper: where A = −1 and β come from
  • In the 5⁺ → 4⁺ transition the electron and antineutrino together carry one unit of angular momentum along the nuclear spin, so both spins point along it. The antineutrino's spin is along its motion, so it goes along the spin. The electron's helicity is ≈ −β, so it leaves mostly against it. That gives A = −1 and the factor β.
  • The real experiment also had γ-ray detectors, which monitored P as the crystal warmed. The sim has none; it takes P from T.
09

Summary

In one line. Aligned ⁶⁰Co nuclei emit electrons mostly against their spin, so reversing the field changes a fixed counter's rate by a fraction 𝒜 = P·β̄·Q; in a mirror-symmetric world 𝒜 would be 0.

Key points

  • Alignment needs millikelvin temperatures: P = B5(C/T), 0.60 at 3 mK, 0.002 at 1 K.
  • The emission weight is W(θ) = 1 + A·P·β·cos θ, with A = −1.
  • Two field directions give 𝒜 ≈ 0.47 P, with error ≈ 1/√N.
  • The mirror image of a B ↑ run is a B ↓ run, so a non-zero 𝒜 means parity is violated.

Common mix-ups

  • "Reversing B changes the physics of the decay." The decay law is the same. Only the spin direction relative to the fixed counter changes.
  • "A warm source shows no parity violation." Each decay is still lopsided relative to its own spin; random spin directions average it out.
  • "𝒜 should be 1, since A = −1." 𝒜 = P·β̄·Q, with P below 1, β̄ = 0.49 and a counter that is not a point.

Things to try on your own

  • Record a B ↑ and a B ↓ run and compare the measured and expected 𝒜. Repeat a few times and compare the spread of 𝒜 with the ± shown.
  • Use the table in section 05 to predict the B ↑ point at minute 3, then check it on the rate plot.
  • After both runs, turn on Mirror image and read the line at the bottom of the canvas.
